content: The air waybill has already been completed. It is standard practice in the shipping industry for the shipper or their agent/freight forwarder to prepare the air waybill. The format of the air waybill varies depending on the operator and country. Similar to the Dangerous Goods Transport Document (DGTD), the air waybill includes general sections detailing shipment information, such as the names and addresses of the shipper and receiver, carrier details, and the quantities and types of packages. However, for infectious substances, two critical sections must be carefully completed: 1. Handling Information Box: For Category A infectious substances, the statement Dangerous Goods as per associated Shipper's Declaration must be included. If the volume of the substance is between 50 mL and 4 L, or the weight is between 50 g and 4 kg, the statement Cargo Aircraft Only or CAO must also be provided. For Category B infectious substances, the name and telephone number of a responsible person knowledgeable about the shipment and available throughout the shipping process must be included on the air waybill or the package. 2. Nature and Quantity of Goods Box: For Category A infectious substances, a general description of the substance, such as laboratory samples, pathology samples, or infectious substance, can be provided. For Category B infectious substances, the UN number, proper shipping name (e.g., UN 3373 Biological Substance, Category B), and the number of packages must be provided unless these are the only packages in the consignment. If the substance is shipped with dry ice, the UN number, proper shipping name, and net quantity of dry ice must also be included. All air shipments, even those not containing dangerous goods, must be accompanied by an air waybill. Even exempt human and animal specimens, which are not subject to other regulations, may require an air waybill. For these shipments, the phrase exempt specimens should be included in the Nature and Quantity of Goods box. If shipped with a coolant, the proper shipping name, UN number, and net quantity of the coolant in the package must also be provided. In the event of a spill involving infectious substances, emergency response information must be readily available to relevant personnel. The following spill clean-up procedure, adapted from the WHO Laboratory Biosafety Manual (4th edition, 2004), provides guidance for handling such incidents: 1. Wear gloves and protective clothing, including face and eye protection if necessary. 2. Cover the spill with a cloth or paper towels to contain it. 3. Pour an appropriate disinfectant over the cloth or paper towels and the surrounding area. A 5% bleach solution is generally suitable, but quaternary ammonium disinfectants should be used for spills on aircraft. 4. Apply the disinfectant concentrically, starting from the outer margin of the spill area and working towards the center. 5. After approximately 30 minutes, remove the materials. If broken glass or sharps are involved, use a dustpan or stiff cardboard to collect the materials and place them in a puncture-resistant container for disposal. 6. Clean and disinfect the spill area. Repeat steps 2–5 if necessary. 7. Dispose of contaminated materials in a leak-proof, puncture-resistant waste disposal container. 8. After successful disinfection, report the incident to the competent authority and inform them that the site has been decontaminated. For detailed information on disinfectants and their recommended use, refer to the WHO Laboratory Biosafety Manual (4th edition, 2020). Special provisions may apply to certain shipments of infectious substances. These provisions supplement or modify standard regulations to ensure the appropriate transport of dangerous goods. Examples include exemptions for aqueous solutions with less than 24% alcohol by volume, genetically modified organisms (GMOs) packed according to specific instructions, and substances not meeting the criteria for dangerous goods classification. Additionally, specific provisions address the transport of medical waste, dry ice, and refrigerated liquid nitrogen, among others. For Category A infectious substances, the proper shipping name must be supplemented with the technical name in documentation. If the infectious substances are unknown but suspected to meet Category A criteria, the words suspected Category A infectious substance must be included in parentheses following the proper shipping name on the transport document. Air transport-specific provisions may require prior approval from relevant authorities for certain shipments, such as medical waste affecting humans or animals. Packaging tests may not be necessary for some items, and quantity limits may not apply to body parts, organs, or whole bodies. When dry ice is used as a refrigerant, the packaging must allow for venting to prevent pressure build-up. Insulated packaging containing fully absorbed refrigerated liquid nitrogen is exempt from dangerous goods regulations if designed to prevent pressure build-up and release of liquid nitrogen. For COVID-19 vaccine shipments accompanied by data loggers or cargo tracking devices with lithium batteries, specific marking and documentation requirements may not apply.
